Content:
Suppose we are given an [MATH: n \!\times\! n] invertible matrix [MATH: A.] Remember that if [MATH: A] is invertible, then the equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}] has only the trivial solution [MATH: \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.]

Content:
Let's extract all possible information from this fact using the vector spaces related to the matrix, namely, the column space and the null space.

Content:
- The fact that the unique solution to [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}] is [MATH: \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}] tells us that [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A)=\{ \mathbf{0} \},] or alternatively, [MATH: \textrm{dim(Null}(A)) = \textrm{nullity}(A)=0.]
- Furthermore, if [MATH: \textrm{dim(Null}(A))=0] then [MATH: A] has no non-pivot columns, or equivalently, all the columns of [MATH: A] are pivot columns. So [MATH: \textrm{dim(Col}(A))=\textrm{rank}(A)=n.]
- Finally, since [MATH: \textrm{Col}(A)] is a subspace of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] and its basis has [MATH: n] linearly independent vectors, we can conclude that [MATH: \textrm{Col}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n.]

Content:
All the results mentioned above can be summarized in the following theorem, called the invertible matrix theorem:

Content:
> Let [MATH: A] be an [MATH: n \!\times\! n] matrix. Then we have the following equivalence:
> [MATH: Col(A) = R^{n}; dim(Col(A)) = n = rank(A); Null(A) = {0}; dim(Null(A)) = 0 = nullity(A)]

  • Statement III is false. Since [MATH: A] is not invertible, then by the invertible matrix theorem, we must have [MATH: \textrm{rank}(A) \neq 4.]
